use_example.english: I speak English — and I am learning French.

summary.takeaway: die Sprache is sprechen's k→ch noun; every language name is a country name + -isch; -isch and -ish are one suffix (*-iskaz); language nouns are capitalized: Ich spreche Französisch.

title: Plurals & i-Mutation
subtitle: Mann→Männer is man→men: umlaut is English's fossil and German's living tool

use_example.german: Die Männer trinken Bier und die Frauen trinken Tee.
use_example.english: The men drink beer and the women drink tea.

summary.takeaway: Umlaut is English's own fossil — Mann/Männer ↔ man/men — and five patterns cover the plural system.

title: den / einen / ihn Case Gym
subtitle: Eighteen accusative-object drills with the table words you own

use_example.german: Ich habe einen Traum.
use_example.english: I have a dream.

summary.takeaway: Masculine objects pay the -n toll (der → den, ein → einen); feminine and neuter stay unchanged.

title: Tochter: Double Shift Showdown
subtitle: Words carrying both D→T and GH→CH — discrimination drills

use_example.german: Die Tochter dachte in der Nacht.
use_example.english: The daughter thought at night.

summary.takeaway: The ch ending is constant — the English front (d, th, or nothing) reports how many laws fired.

title: Blood & Kin
subtitle: Vater ↔ father (Verner's law, not V→B), Mutter, Sohn, Tochter — the family as cognate wall

use_example.german: Mein Vater ist alt, aber meine Mutter ist Lehrerin.
use_example.english: My father is old, but my mother is a teacher.

summary.takeaway: Mutter, Sohn, Bruder, Schwester, Tochter — all twins; Vater wears Verner's law; Eltern is 'the elder ones' frozen into a noun.

title: Richtung I: links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten
subtitle: left, right, and the words that point the way — one twin, one loner, three builders

use_example.german: Gehen Sie geradeaus — die Kirche ist links, wir wohnen oben.
use_example.english: Go straight ahead — the church is on the left, we live upstairs.

summary.takeaway: rechts/right is one word (*rehtaz, with recht, Licht, Nacht, acht), links has no English twin, geradeaus is gerade+aus, and oben/unten are the adverbs of über/over and unter/under.

title: Richtung II: hinten, Norden, Osten, Westen, Süden
subtitle: behind, and the four compass points — dawn, evening, sun-side and the left hand

use_example.german: Der Zug kommt um zehn Uhr aus dem Süden.
use_example.english: The train comes from the south at ten o'clock.

summary.takeaway: hinten is behind's twin — German built it with a t-suffix, not the D→T shift; Norden, Osten, Westen and Süden are pure sky twins — dawn, evening, sun-side and the left hand.

title: Entfernung: die Nähe, weit, fern, quer, entlang
subtitle: near and far on one axis — and the two words that walk a path instead of pointing at a place

use_example.german: Wie weit ist der Strand? — Zehn Minuten zu Fuß.
use_example.english: How far is the beach? — Ten minutes on foot.

summary.takeaway: die Nähe ↔ nigh, weit ↔ wide, fern ↔ far, entlang = ent + lang — one axis, two path words, and entlang always last.

title: Essen I: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse
subtitle: the table's backbone — two sound twins, two Latin guests, and one word English never touched

use_example.german: Zu Ostern essen wir Fisch — am Freitag essen wir immer Fisch.
use_example.english: At Easter we eat fish — on Friday we always eat fish.

summary.takeaway: Fisch and Fleisch are twins (English narrowed Fleisch to flesh), Käse and Suppe are shared Latin loans, Gemüse grew alone in German — and the genders stand: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse.

title: Farben I: rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt
subtitle: the first row of colors — three twins, one half-lost twin, and the honest odd one out

use_example.german: Im Dezember ist der Berg weiß — null Blumen, aber der Himmel ist blau.
use_example.english: In December the mountain is white — zero flowers, but the sky is blue.

summary.takeaway: rot wears D→T (red kept the D), blau and grün are pure twins, schwarz survives in English only as swarthy, bunt's origin is honestly unknown — and weiß is white with the T→S badge.

title: Article Gym: 20 Nouns, 3 Colors
subtitle: Rapid der/die/das assignment with every table noun you have met

use_example.german: Die Zeit ist kurz.
use_example.english: The time is short.

summary.takeaway: Gender is collected with the word, flagged in color — reps build the reflex before rules explain it.

title: W-Word Cognate Set
subtitle: All eight W-words matched to their English twins — and the wer≠where trap

use_example.german: Wie laut ist die Katze?
use_example.english: How loud is the cat?

summary.takeaway: The W-words are one family — English wh-, German w- — and the trap is structural: wer=who, wo=where.

title: weil & dass: the Verb Waits
subtitle: Twelve subclauses built on the two doors — verb-final, every time

use_example.german: Ich weiß, dass du morgen kommst.
use_example.english: I know that you are coming tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: weil and dass open the basement: the conjugated verb waits at the very end — Old English's habit, German's law.

title: V→B Word Hunt
subtitle: Atlas-bridged derivation drills across the whole quiet family

use_example.german: Wir glauben, wir leben, wir lieben.
use_example.english: We believe, we live, we love.

summary.takeaway: English v/f between vowels → German b: thirteen words from verbs to ravens, one law end to end.

title: K→CH Discrimination Drills
subtitle: Predict the ch-sound, derive unseen forms, and catch the k-impostors

use_example.german: Der Koch findet den Kuchen süß.
use_example.english: The cook finds the cake sweet.

summary.takeaway: The vowel steers the ch-sound; loanwords keep k; and Kirche, Rauch, acht, Recht are English gh-words still sounding their ghost.

title: Preposition Sentence Ladders
subtitle: Full sentences chaining prepositional phrases onto taught verbs

use_example.german: Morgen fahre ich mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
use_example.english: Tomorrow I travel by train to Berlin.

summary.takeaway: Time, Manner, Place — each phrase with its own case law, stacked on a V2 spine. The last drill; the sentences build themselves now.

title: Reisen I: das Fahrrad, der Koffer, die Karte, die Haltestelle, das Dorf
subtitle: wheels, luggage and the road out of town — a travel kit built from verbs and baskets you already own

use_example.german: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad ins Dorf — der Koffer ist zu schwer.
use_example.english: I go to the village by bike — the suitcase is too heavy.

summary.takeaway: Fahrrad = fahren + Rad; Koffer is coffin's Latin cousin (cophinus); Karte is card/chart from charta; Haltestelle hides halten (hold, D→T); Dorf is thorpe with the TH→D badge.

title: Hobbys II: die Party, die Gitarre, reiten, das Schach, die Freizeit
subtitle: the party set — a Persian king, a Greek harp, and the free time you already speak

use_example.german: Endlich kommt die Freizeit — wir tanzen auf der Party.
use_example.english: Finally the free time comes — we dance at the party.

summary.takeaway: die Gitarre and guitar share a Greek kithara, das Schach is the Persian shāh, reiten ritt geritten is ride rode ridden — and die Freizeit is free + tide.

title: Gefühle: die Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, die Freude
subtitle: love you already own, nice you already bought — and the proud ones with no twin

use_example.german: Ich bin stolz auf das Haus — die Musik macht Freude.
use_example.english: I am proud of the house — the music brings joy.

summary.takeaway: die Liebe is love's twin with the b, nett is neat gone warm, die Freude is frolic's German home — and stolz has no twin: English bought French proud.

title: Capstone: The Bridge Reading
subtitle: Ein Tag in Berlin — one connected story built from everything you own

use_example.german: Es gibt keinen besseren Morgen.
use_example.english: There is no better morning.

summary.takeaway: You crossed the bridge: sixty words, every one decoded by a law you own — the trail ends, the language begins.

title: Länder I: Deutschland, Frankreich, England, Spanien, Italien
subtitle: five country names — the ones English kept, the ones it renamed, and the one that points at you

use_example.german: Ich wohne in Deutschland — mein Bruder wohnt in England.
use_example.english: I live in Germany — my brother lives in England.

summary.takeaway: England is the Angles' land from Angeln; deutsch and Dutch are one word (*þiudiskaz, TH→D); reich is rich (k→ch); Frankreich is the Franks' realm; Spanien and Italien are Rome's own names.

title: Berufe III: der Ingenieur, der Friseur, der Beruf, der Pilot, der Kellner
subtitle: where English borrowed hardest — and Beruf, vocation translated rather than inherited

use_example.german: Was sind Sie von Beruf? — Ich bin Pilot.
use_example.english: What do you do for a living? — I am a pilot.

summary.takeaway: Ingenieur and engineer are the same French word (Latin ingenium, the mind's engine); Friseur is the curler; Pilot is the French-Italian loan English shares; Kellner is the man of the Keller, twin of cellar; Beruf is vocation translated, not inherited.

title: Hobbys I: die Musik, der Sport, das Lied, tanzen, malen
subtitle: what you do when the work stops — and the word German borrowed back from English

use_example.german: Mein Hobby ist Musik — ich tanze selten, ich singe oft.
use_example.english: My hobby is music — I seldom dance, I often sing.

summary.takeaway: die Musik is the Muses' art, der Sport is English's own word sold back to German, das Lied's Old English twin leod is lost — and tanzen/dance are the same French purchase.

title: Adjektive: richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen
subtitle: five adjectives English kept almost intact — and the proof that German is English in other sounds

use_example.german: Der Gast geht, das Haus ist leer — die Tür zum Balkon ist offen.
use_example.english: The guest leaves, the house is empty — the door to the balcony is open.

summary.takeaway: richtig is right with the gh↔ch badge, falsch is Latin falsus bought twice, offen is open with the shift working in its middle (p became ff, as in Apfel) — and sauber and leer have no twins: even sisters have words the other never had.

title: Reisen II: die Fahrkarte, der Fahrplan, die Abfahrt, die Ankunft, der Flughafen
subtitle: the timetable set — German compounds it from three verbs, English borrowed it from Latin

use_example.german: Die Abfahrt ist um acht Uhr — die Ankunft ist spät.
use_example.english: The departure is at eight o'clock — the arrival is late.

summary.takeaway: Abfahrt = ab (English off) + Fahrt (fare); Ankunft = an + Kunft, kommen's frozen noun and flight's twin; Flughafen = Flug + Hafen (haven). English borrowed Latin for all of it.

title: Frühstück: das Frühstück, das Brötchen, die Marmelade, der Toast, die Butter
subtitle: the one meal with its own noun — and butter coming back as a compound

use_example.german: Das Frühstück dauert zwanzig Minuten — Brot mit Butter und Marmelade.
use_example.english: Breakfast lasts twenty minutes — bread with butter and jam.

summary.takeaway: Frühstück is früh + Stück, 'early piece' (English named the broken fast instead), Brötchen is the -chen little bread, Marmelade hides Greek honey, Toast is English's Latin — and Butterbrot is butter + Brot, both lesson-101 words.

title: Berufe II: der Student, der Fahrer, der Sänger, der Bauer, der Arbeiter
subtitle: the -er jobs do what English -er does — and Bauer turns out to be the dweller inside neighbor

use_example.german: Der Sänger singt schön — der Fahrer fährt den Bus.
use_example.english: The singer sings beautifully — the driver drives the bus.

summary.takeaway: -er does English -er's work on both sides; singen-sang-gesungen mirrors sing-sang-sung; Bauer is the dweller in neighbor and boor; Student is studēre's person; Arbeit has no English twin — work's twin is Werk.

title: Menschen: wir, die Schule, der Gast, die Gruppe, der Held
subtitle: we, school, guest, group, hero — and the ancient word that means stranger and friend

use_example.german: Wir wohnen in Deutschland, und der Gast kommt aus England.
use_example.english: We live in Germany, and the guest comes from England.

summary.takeaway: wir is we, der Gast and guest share a root with hostile, der Held is the Old English hæleþ English lost — and das Dorf wears the TH→D badge as thorp.

title: Reisen III: der Ausflug, der Tourist, das Gepäck, der Pass, die Fähre
subtitle: the day-trip kit — an out-flight, a passport named for walking, and the fahren family's boat

use_example.german: Wir machen einen Ausflug — die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
use_example.english: We take an excursion — the ferry goes across the river.

summary.takeaway: Ausflug = aus + Flug (excursion is Latin 'run out'); Gepäck is the ge-collective of English pack; Pass is Latin passus 'step'; Fähre is ferry of the fahren family; Tourist is a turner of circles.

title: Länder II: die Schweiz, Österreich, die Türkei, Polen, Irland
subtitle: five more countries — two insist on their article, and the endings -ei, -land and -reich still mean what they meant

use_example.german: Im März fahre ich nach Österreich — im Januar war ich in der Schweiz.
use_example.english: In March I am traveling to Austria — in January I was in Switzerland.

summary.takeaway: die Schweiz and die Türkei wear die; Österreich, Polen and Irland go bare. Österreich is 'eastern realm' with rich inside it, die Türkei is Türk + -ei like Bäckerei, and Irland kept Ireland's name.

title: Max läuft weg
subtitle: A present-tense story: a dog, an open door, and a happy ending
label: s1

use_example.german: Max läuft in die Stadt. Paul sucht ihn überall.
use_example.english: Max runs into the city. Paul searches for him everywhere.

summary.takeaway: A story is a chain of small sentences: who does what, where it happens, and how it ends. You do not need every word to follow the chain.

title: Der kleine Hund
subtitle: Anna finds a lost puppy and follows him to the person who misses him

use_example.german: Der Hund sitzt allein unter einem Baum. Anna folgt ihm zu einem alten Mann.
use_example.english: The dog sits alone under a tree. Anna follows him to an old man.

summary.takeaway: Weather and feelings are story clues. A sunny start and a sad old man tell you the problem before the dialogue names it.

title: Eine Reise mit Pannen
subtitle: A trip to Paris goes wrong in small ways — and becomes a memory
label: s2

use_example.german: Sie haben den falschen Bus genommen, aber dann einen schönen Markt gefunden.
use_example.english: They took the wrong bus, but then found a beautiful market.

summary.takeaway: In a Perfekt story, the participle at the end is the action; the auxiliary at the front only carries the time. Read the bracket as one unit.

title: Ein Tag im Park
subtitle: A Perfekt diary of one ordinary Saturday with a friend and a dog

use_example.german: Um zehn Uhr haben sie sich im Park getroffen, und um eins sind sie nach Hause gegangen.
use_example.english: At ten they met in the park, and at one they went home.

summary.takeaway: Time phrases are the skeleton of a past-tense story. Find the clock words first; the participles then hang on them.

title: Fahrrad statt Auto
subtitle: Tom's car breaks down, and a borrowed bicycle changes his mind
label: s3

use_example.german: Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto, und es ist gut für meine Gesundheit.
use_example.english: That is faster than by car, and it is good for my health.

summary.takeaway: Comparisons carry a story's argument: schneller als, langsamer als, gleich schnell wie. Find the hinge word and you find the claim.

title: Die Verspätung
subtitle: Lukas is late to a birthday — and the reason is not what Sarah thinks
label: s4

use_example.german: Der Bus war kaputt, und Lukas ist zu spät gekommen.
use_example.english: The bus was broken, and Lukas arrived too late.

summary.takeaway: A story's mood can turn on one sentence. Sarah's laughter changes 'angry girlfriend' into 'joke' — read for that turn.

title: Das Geheimnis der Bibliothek
subtitle: A book falls in a library-bar, and a letter hides a treasure

use_example.german: Sie finden den Schatz nicht, aber sie sind trotzdem glücklich.
use_example.english: They do not find the treasure, but they are happy all the same.

summary.takeaway: A mystery can end without a solution. The story's job is to make the search interesting, not to hand you the treasure.

title: Max und der kranke Montag
subtitle: Max pretends to be sick — his mother's thermometer has other ideas
label: s5

use_example.german: Er hat gesagt, dass er krank ist, aber seine Mutter hat kein Fieber gefunden.
use_example.english: He said that he is sick, but his mother found no fever.

summary.takeaway: A story can be a small argument: claim, evidence, verdict. The dass-clause puts the verdict's verb at the end, where the evidence lands.

title: Der rote Schal
subtitle: A red scarf disappears at the market — and a stranger brings it back

use_example.german: Mia sucht ihren Schal. Ein Junge findet ihn unter einem Tisch.
use_example.english: Mia looks for her scarf. A boy finds it under a table.

summary.takeaway: A lost-object story is built from place words: auf dem Markt, in der Tasche, unter dem Tisch. Follow the places and the object reappears.

title: Der Ausflug zum See
subtitle: A family trip to a lake: sun, swimming, rain, and a tree

use_example.german: Der See ist größer als der Fluss, und am Nachmittag hat es geregnet.
use_example.english: The lake is bigger than the river, and in the afternoon it rained.

summary.takeaway: Weather and comparisons give a trip story its shape: a sunny morning, a rainy afternoon, and a warm conclusion.
